sector: Medicinal Cannabis / DELISTED - IN RECEIVERSHIP (heading to liquidation)

status.summary: Cannasouth is NOT a going-concern operating company and this is NOT a normal equity investment candidate. The NZX-listed parent entity was placed into voluntary administration on 28 March 2024, moved into a Deed of Company Arrangement (DOCA) with creditors in June 2024, was DELISTED from the NZX Main Board on 17 December 2024, and was placed into RECEIVERSHIP on 22 May 2025 (Kevin Davies, Principle Insolvency, appointed by the DOCA funders). The receiver has stated the company is heading for liquidation. Operating subsidiaries Cannasouth Cultivation and Eqalis Group were sold in a receivership asset sale (reported February 2026) to a newly formed entity, Marshall Road Holdings, for NZ$4.7 million — proceeds that were INSUFFICIENT to repay the ~$2.53 million owed to secured (GSA) noteholders in full, let alone the ~$109,000 owed to unsecured creditors or anything to ordinary shareholders. There is no functioning secondary market for CBD.NZ shares; the last NZX trade was NZ$0.098 shortly before the 17 December 2024 delisting, and that price is a stale, non-transactable historical artifact, not a current valuation. This file exists purely as a factual record for a failed listing; it is not a buy/hold/sell recommendation on a live security.
status.expected_shareholder_recovery: Nil. Secured GSA noteholders (~$2.53m) rank ahead of unsecured creditors (~$109k), who in turn rank ahead of ordinary shareholders. The February 2026 sale of the operating subsidiaries to Marshall Road Holdings for $4.7m was reported by the receiver as insufficient to repay secured noteholders in full, meaning there is a shortfall even at the top of the creditor stack. Ordinary equity is at the very bottom of that stack and recovers nothing under any disclosed scenario.

overview: Cannasouth Limited was a Hamilton, New Zealand-based, vertically integrated medicinal cannabis company that listed on the NZX Main Board in June 2019 as the first cannabis company on the exchange, raising roughly NZ$30 million from shareholders over its life. It operated cannabis cultivation (Cannasouth Cultivation, a purpose-built Waikato glasshouse), extraction and manufacturing (Cannasouth Bioscience), and briefly a liquid-filling pharmaceutical subsidiary (Midwest Pharmaceutics, divested to Harker Herbals in 2023), and merged with Bay of Plenty-based Eqalis Group New Zealand in June 2023 to try to build scale. The company never achieved meaningful revenue, burned through its capital in a costly, multi-year, capital-intensive cultivation and GMP-certification build-out, and collapsed into voluntary administration in March 2024, a DOCA in June 2024, delisting from the NZX in December 2024, and receivership in May 2025, with the receiver stating liquidation is the expected next step.

business_model.summary: Historically pre-revenue to nominal-revenue: FY2022 operating revenue and other income was just NZ$140,601 (FY2021 restated NZ$205,772), against a total loss of NZ$7.92-8.22 million (FY2021 loss ~NZ$3.12 million), and FY2023 revenue reached only ~NZ$956,000 against an NZ$8.8 million full-year loss. The intended model was vertically integrated medicinal cannabis: cultivate GACP/GMP-certified cannabis flower and biomass domestically, extract and manufacture cannabis-based ingredients and finished medicines (oils, tinctures, oral solutions), and sell into the small (but growing) NZ prescription market plus export to Australia and Germany. This required years of capital-intensive glasshouse construction, licensing and GMP certification before any offsetting revenue arrived, and the company never closed that gap before running out of funding. As of August 2026 there is no ongoing business model to speak of for the listed entity — its subsidiaries have been sold out of receivership to a new private owner (Marshall Road Holdings) and the listed shell itself is being wound down.

competitive_position.market_position: Formerly positioned as an early-mover, vertically integrated aspirant to be New Zealand's leading fully operational medicinal cannabis company; in practice never reached sustainable scale or profitability and is now defunct as a listed entity. Its operating assets (post-receivership) are now privately owned by Marshall Road Holdings, outside the listed vehicle.

moat_factors.factor: First-mover NZX listing / early GACP-certified cultivation facility
moat_factors.description: Being first-to-market and holding one of NZ's few GACP/GMP-certified cultivation and manufacturing facilities provided some regulatory and reputational head start, but it was not sufficient to generate revenue at a scale that could fund the capital-intensive build-out, and the asset base has since been sold out of the listed company via receivership.

The Eqalis merger aimed to combine flower/biomass production with ingredient manufacturing and finished-product distribution, but this scale never translated into profitability before the funding crisis hit.

weaknesses: Essentially pre-revenue for its entire listed life relative to its cost base - FY2022 revenue of $140,601 against an $7.92-8.22 million loss is illustrative of a structurally unviable unit economics gap that was never closed

Extremely capital-intensive cultivation build (glasshouse, GACP/GMP certification) with a multi-year lag before any offsetting revenue, funded by repeated shareholder capital raises and ultimately convertible/secured notes

Governance and funding breakdown: directors cited an inability to secure additional funding and an inability to balance the competing interests of ordinary shareholders versus convertible noteholders, precipitating the March 2024 voluntary administration
Total loss of the NZX listing (December 2024) removed any public market liquidity or price discovery for existing shareholders

Operating subsidiaries were ultimately sold out of receivership for NZ$4.7 million (February 2026) - a fraction of the ~$30 million shareholders originally invested, and even that sum proved insufficient to fully repay secured noteholders, before unsecured creditors or shareholders see anything

growth_drivers: NONE APPLICABLE - the listed entity is defunct, in receivership, and heading toward liquidation. There is no growth thesis for CBD.NZ equity.
(Historical, pre-collapse) Domestic prescription volume growth under NZ's Medicinal Cannabis Scheme as more patients transitioned from black-market to legal supply
(Historical, pre-collapse) Export expansion into Australia and Germany, and the Eqalis merger's aim to create the largest vertically integrated NZ medicinal cannabis company

(Post-receivership, NOT relevant to CBD.NZ shareholders) The underlying cultivation and manufacturing assets continue operating under new private ownership (Marshall Road Holdings), so the physical business may yet succeed - but any future value accrues entirely to the new owner, not to Cannasouth Limited's original shareholders or the delisted CBD.NZ stock

business.risk: Entity is in receivership and expected to be liquidated
business.description: Receiver Kevin Davies (Principle Insolvency) has publicly stated Cannasouth is heading for liquidation once the receivership process concludes. There is no ongoing operating business inside the listed entity.

CBD.NZ was delisted from the NZX Main Board on 17 December 2024 for multiple listing-rule breaches (unpaid listing fees, non-compliant board composition, failure to file audited annual reports). There is no NZX quote, no market maker, and no confirmed off-market/unlisted trading facility has been established despite the delisting announcement flagging the new board would explore one. Any holding is effectively illiquid and unsaleable through normal channels.

Reporting at the time of the receivership appointment (May 2025) stated shareholders who invested approximately NZ$30 million over the company's life 'will lose the lot.' The subsequent February 2026 news that the $4.7 million sale of operating subsidiaries to Marshall Road Holdings was insufficient even to repay secured noteholders in full confirms there is no residual value for equity.

business.risk: Failed capital raise and shareholder/noteholder conflict
business.description: The precipitating cause of the 2024 collapse was a failed attempt to raise $5 million on the sharemarket and misalignment between shareholders and directors over financing options, followed by noteholders effectively seizing control as the company tipped into receivership.

financial.risk: Secured creditors rank ahead of shareholders and are themselves under-recovered
financial.description: Holders of a General Security Agreement (GSA) over the company's assets were owed approximately $2.53 million as of the first receiver's report (mid-2025); unsecured creditors were owed a further ~$109,000. The February 2026 asset sale proceeds of $4.7 million were reported as insufficient to fully repay secured noteholders, meaning there is a shortfall at the top of the payment waterfall before unsecured creditors or ordinary shareholders are considered at all.

financial.risk: Accumulated losses and cash depletion pre-collapse
financial.description: Accumulated deficit reached NZ$17.4 million at 31 December 2022; cash fell from $5.5 million to $1.9 million during FY2022 alone; FY2023 full-year loss was $8.8 million. This trajectory of unfunded capital-intensive growth directly preceded the 2024 insolvency.

regulatory.description: NZ RegCo approved delisting effective 17 December 2024 citing unpaid listing fees, a non-compliant board, and failure to file audited annual reports - governance and compliance failures compounding the underlying financial distress.

regulatory.risk: Onerous NZ Medicinal Cannabis Scheme regulatory burden
regulatory.description: The receiver has publicly criticised New Zealand's medicinal cannabis regulations as 'unbalanced, commercially unfair, and anti-competitive,' arguing they are 'crushing' legitimate operators - a sector-wide regulatory critique voiced after Cannasouth's collapse, echoed by the near-simultaneous failures of Greenfern Industries (receivership Feb 2025) and Helius Therapeutics (collapse reported March 2026).

macro.risk: Sector-wide collapse of NZX-listed medicinal cannabis
macro.description: Cannasouth's failure was not idiosyncratic: Greenfern Industries collapsed into receivership in February 2025 (owing $1.2m and destroying ~$10.5m of shareholder capital), and Helius Therapeutics' collapse (reported March 2026) has been described in NZ media as marking the end of the country's 'big cannabis era.' Persistent oversupply, low domestic prescription volumes relative to installed cultivation capacity, high compliance/GMP costs, and reliance on export markets that did not materialise at scale afflicted the whole NZX cannabis cohort, not just Cannasouth.

macro.risk: Illiquid, unfunded small-cap capital markets for pre-revenue growth stories
macro.description: Cannasouth's fatal capital raise failure in 2023-24 reflected broader NZX small-cap investor fatigue with capital-hungry, pre-revenue growth stories, compounding sector-specific headwinds.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The NZX-listed medicinal cannabis cohort has effectively been wiped out: Cannasouth (delisted Dec 2024, receivership May 2025, heading to liquidation), Greenfern Industries (receivership Feb 2025), and Helius Therapeutics (collapse reported March 2026) have all failed within roughly a two-year window, described in NZ financial media as the end of the country's 'big cannabis era.' The underlying NZ Medicinal Cannabis Scheme market itself may continue to grow in prescription volumes, but the operators that built out early-stage domestic cultivation/manufacturing capacity ahead of demand and export traction have not survived as listed public companies.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Not meaningfully applicable - the listed entity is defunct. Historically, the underlying medicinal cannabis growth story was a structural/secular one (legalisation, prescription growth) rather than macro-cyclical, but capital intensity made the sector highly sensitive to funding-market conditions, and NZ small-cap risk appetite dried up before any of the major domestic players reached self-sustaining profitability.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: N/A for equity - the company is in receivership. Historically, its reliance on convertible/secured notes as a late-stage funding source made it acutely sensitive to the cost and availability of debt capital, which contributed to the funding crisis.

guidance.management_commentary: There is no current operating management issuing guidance. The receiver, Kevin Davies of Principle Insolvency, has publicly stated Cannasouth is heading toward liquidation and has criticised New Zealand's medicinal cannabis regulatory regime as 'unbalanced, commercially unfair, and anticompetitive.'

bull_case: There is essentially NO credible bull case for CBD.NZ equity holders. The only theoretical scenario is a highly speculative residual-recovery outcome in liquidation - e.g. if final liquidator costs and any recovered/disputed related-party amounts somehow left a surplus after secured and unsecured creditors were paid in full - but the disclosed facts (a $4.7 million subsidiary sale already reported as insufficient to repay $2.53 million of secured debt) make this scenario extremely unlikely; probability should be treated as near-zero, not a realistic investment thesis

The underlying medicinal cannabis cultivation and manufacturing assets continue to operate under new private ownership (Marshall Road Holdings), which shows the physical business itself may have some residual commercial viability - but this value now belongs entirely to the new private owner, not to Cannasouth Limited or its original shareholders

Any ongoing liquidator investigation into disputed asset sales or related-party loans could theoretically claw back value for the creditor pool - but even a successful claw-back would need to first clear the secured noteholder shortfall before ordinary shareholders (last in the payment waterfall) could see anything, which the numbers currently disclosed make very unlikely
bear_case: Cannasouth is DELISTED (17 December 2024) and IN RECEIVERSHIP (since 22 May 2025), with the receiver stating publicly that liquidation is the expected outcome - this is not a distressed-but-recoverable equity, it is a failed company with no going-concern business inside the listed entity

Shares are illiquid and effectively untradeable: there is no NZX quote and no confirmed functioning off-market/unlisted trading facility despite the delisting announcement flagging the new board would explore one; the last traded price of NZ$0.098 (17 December 2024) is a stale historical artifact with no bearing on current realisable value

In a receivership/liquidation, secured creditors are paid ahead of unsecured creditors, who are paid ahead of ordinary shareholders. The February 2026 sale of Cannasouth's operating subsidiaries to Marshall Road Holdings for NZ$4.7 million was reported by the receiver as insufficient to fully repay the ~$2.53 million owed to secured GSA noteholders alone - meaning there is a shortfall before unsecured creditors (owed ~$109,000) are considered, let alone shareholders. The expected residual equity value is NIL.
Reporting at the time of the receivership appointment stated plainly that shareholders who invested approximately NZ$30 million into Cannasouth over its listed life 'will lose the lot'

Cannasouth's failure is part of a broader collapse of NZX-listed medicinal cannabis: peer Greenfern Industries also entered receivership (February 2025, destroying ~$10.5m of shareholder capital) and Helius Therapeutics collapsed in early 2026, described in NZ media as the end of the country's 'big cannabis era' - indicating the failure reflects structural sector economics (oversupply, thin domestic prescription volumes, high compliance costs, capital-intensive build-outs ahead of revenue), not merely company-specific mismanagement
